headline: Zoning kept out factories. Then apartments.

portrait.alt: Portrait photograph of Edward M. Bassett in a dark suit, high white collar and tie
portrait.credit: Edward M. Bassett, about 1914. Reuben Leslie Maynard. Public domain.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: A shadow over Broadway
slides.text: Manhattan's tenements lacked light and air, and in 1915 the Equitable Building cast a seven-acre shadow. **Edward M. Bassett set out to bring the light back.**
slides.alt: The Equitable Building, a huge flat-topped office block, towering over Trinity Church and its neighbors in lower Manhattan
slides.credit: Equitable Building, New York City, 1915. Library of Congress. Public domain.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: America's first zoning code
slides.text: His commission wrote the first comprehensive US zoning code in 1916, capping heights and keeping factories out of residential districts. **By 1923, 218 municipalities had zoning.**
slides.alt: Charcoal drawing of a stepped skyscraper mass, its towers narrowing in setbacks as they rise
slides.credit: Study of the largest building the 1916 zoning law allowed, 1922. Hugh Ferriss. Cooper Hewitt. Public domain.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Homes far from everything
slides.statLabel: homes the US was short in 2022, by a Moody's estimate
slides.text: As zoning spread, later codes barred apartments from home districts and kept homes far from jobs. **The rules that kept out factories kept out homes.**

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: A judge warned. The cars came later.
slides.text: Striking down a zoning law, a federal judge wrote that it would "segregate them according to their income." **He warned in 1924 and was overruled in 1926.**

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: Undoing it takes new law
slides.text: In 2019 Oregon required cities over 10,000 people to allow duplexes on single-family land. **Undoing local codes took a state law.**

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: Light and air under towers like the Equitable
Zoning in 218 municipalities with over 22 million people by 1923
costs: A shortfall of more than 1.5 million homes, by one 2022 estimate
Homes, jobs and shops set apart, so people rely on cars (EPA, 2001)
Apartments barred from home districts; Oregon needed a 2019 law to allow duplexes
slides.text: It gave crowded streets light and air and kept factories away from homes. **It cost neighborhoods where jobs and shops need a car.**

slides.label: Pattern
slides.title: Cheap now, paid later
slides.text: In 1916 the light and air arrived at once. **The cost grew as cities spread out under the rules.**

slides.label: Lesson
slides.title: What we take from it
slides.text: A rule written for one city's problem becomes a template for places that never had it. **Give every rule a date to check it again.**
